entries.title: A great name, little to show
entries.literal_meaning: The name is big; the appearance is small.
entries.explanation: The dictionary takes this beyond appearance: a famous name can belong to someone inadequate in practice. The balanced halves puncture an imposing reputation. Our application asks what stands behind an impressive introduction, without making physical size a measure of ability.
entries.meaning_odia: ଅଭିଧାନର ଟୀକା ଏହାକୁ ଦେଖାଶୁଣାଠାରୁ ଆଗକୁ ନିଏ: ବଡ଼ ନାମ ଥାଇ ମଧ୍ୟ କାମରେ ଅଯୋଗ୍ୟତା ଥାଇପାରେ। ଦୁଇ ଖଣ୍ଡର ବିପରୀତତା ଖ୍ୟାତିର ଆଡ଼ମ୍ବରକୁ ଫୁଟାଇ ଦିଏ। ଆମ ପ୍ରୟୋଗରେ ଚମତ୍କାର ପରିଚୟ ପଛରେ କି କାମ ଅଛି, ସେ ପ୍ରଶ୍ନ ଉଠେ; ଶରୀରର ଆକାର ଯୋଗ୍ୟତାର ମାପ ହୁଏନାହିଁ।
entries.english_summary: The source contrasts a large reputation with inadequate performance.

One reader says, “I trusted the name; now let us examine the work.” Another recalls this saying. The book discussion is invented.

entries.title: A headache without a head
entries.literal_meaning: There is no head, yet it has a headache.
entries.explanation: The line removes the head and keeps its ache: an impossible complaint compressed into a joke. The entry separately gives a figurative sense of deep anxiety. Our reading transfers the paradox to worry about a responsibility that does not exist; the source supplies no particular occasion for that use. It does not establish that anyone’s actual pain is false.
entries.meaning_odia: ମୁଣ୍ଡକୁ ବାଦ ଦେଇ ତାହାର ବଥାକୁ ରଖାଯାଇଛି—ଅସମ୍ଭବ ଅଭିଯୋଗଟି ହିଁ ପରିହାସ। ଏହି ଶବ୍ଦର ଅଲଗା ଲକ୍ଷଣାର୍ଥରେ ଗଭୀର ଚିନ୍ତା ଦିଆଯାଇଛି। ଆମ ପଢ଼ାରେ ନଥିବା ଦାୟିତ୍ୱ ନେଇ ଚିନ୍ତାକୁ ଏହି ବିରୋଧାଭାସରେ ଦେଖାଯାଏ; ସେ ପ୍ରୟୋଗର କୌଣସି ନିର୍ଦ୍ଦିଷ୍ଟ ଅବସର ଉତ୍ସ ଦିଏନାହିଁ। କାହାର ପ୍ରକୃତ ଯନ୍ତ୍ରଣା ମିଛ ବୋଲି ଏଥିରୁ ପ୍ରମାଣ ହୁଏନାହିଁ।
entries.english_summary: An impossible headache becomes our analogy for a worry without its supposed responsibility.

entries.title: A fitting pair
entries.literal_meaning: Whatever suits each: soak black gram and rice.
entries.explanation: The entry defines the opening as what is appropriate to a person or thing. Its answer brings black gram and rice together in the action of soaking. Our reading follows the pairing: usefulness can depend on what accompanies something. The quotation names no finished dish, proportion or rule for sorting people into groups.
